code.title: Print the runtime you are on

followUps:
The JVM is the platform-specific one, together with the JRE and JDK builds that contain it. Bytecode and .class files are the same everywhere, but each operating system and CPU needs its own JVM binary (for example Linux aarch64 or Windows x64), because the JVM must turn bytecode into that machine's native instructions.

The JRE and JDK inherit this, since they bundle a JVM and native launcher. Your .jar is portable; the runtime you install is not.

Build a trimmed runtime with jlink and copy only that into a small base image. Steps: run jdeps to list needed modules, then jlink --add-modules java.base,java.logging --strip-debug --no-header-files --no-man-pages --output /rt, and use a multi-stage Docker build.

FROM eclipse-temurin:25 AS build
RUN jlink --add-modules java.base --strip-debug --output /rt
FROM debian:stable-slim
COPY --from=build /rt /rt

A full JDK is roughly 300 MB; a jlink image with a few modules is often 40 to 60 MB.

Yes. A .class file is already compiled bytecode, so the JRE, which contains the JVM and class library, can run it with java -cp out Main. You only need the JDK to create it with javac.

Since JDK 11 there is no separate JRE download, so in practice you run it with the JDK or a jlink image, which behaves like a JRE. The java launcher is the tool doing the work in all cases.

code.title: Fixed sizes, platform-dependent separators

followUps:
Bytecode is the compact instruction set the JVM executes, produced by javac. Compile int add(int a,int b){return a+b;} and run javap -c Main.

iload_1
iload_2
iadd
ireturn

Each line is one instruction working on a stack: push a, push b, add the top two, return the result. javap -v also shows the constant pool and the class version number.

Anything that touches the operating system directly can differ, even though the bytecode is identical. Examples: line endings (\r\n on Windows, \n on Linux), path separators (\ vs /), case-sensitive file names, default charset on old JDKs, available native libraries through JNI, file locking rules, and time zone data.

Fix them by using Path, System.lineSeparator(), explicit charsets, and testing on both systems in CI.

code.title: main overloading and static init order

followUps:
Because the exit status is a property of the whole process, not of one method, and Java threads may keep running after main returns. A returned int would be wrong when other non-daemon threads are still working.

So Java uses System.exit(n) to choose the status explicitly, and otherwise exits with 0 once all non-daemon threads finish, or 1 if an exception escapes. Example: if (bad) System.exit(2); sets the code to 2 and starts shutdown hooks.

The class's static initializers (static fields with initial values and static { } blocks) run first, because the class must be initialized before its static method is invoked. Before that, the class is loaded, verified and prepared with default values.

static int x = 5;
static { System.out.println("init " + x); }

This prints init 5 before any line in main. Instance initializers do not run unless you create an object.

Read it with System.getProperty("mode"), which returns the value passed as java -Dmode=prod Main. It returns null if the option was not given, so supply a default: System.getProperty("mode", "dev").

Related helpers are Integer.getInteger("port", 8080) and Boolean.getBoolean("debug"). Environment variables are different: use System.getenv("MODE").

code.title: Primitive ranges and defaults

followUps:
1000 bytes in practice on HotSpot, because each boolean element in an array takes one byte, though the language specification does not fix the size. Add about 16 bytes of array header, so roughly 1016 bytes in total, rounded up to a multiple of 8.

If you need 1000 flags in 125 bytes, use a BitSet, which packs 64 flags into each long.

Pick float when memory or bandwidth matters more than precision, such as large arrays of graphics, sensor or machine learning data, where 7 digits are enough. A float[1_000_000] uses 4 MB while a double[1_000_000] uses 8 MB.

Do not use float for money or for long running sums, since it has only about 7 significant digits: 16777216f + 1f still equals 16777216. Default to double otherwise.

Because two's complement uses the same 256 bit patterns for negative and non-negative values, and zero takes one of the non-negative patterns. That leaves 128 patterns for negatives (-128 to -1) and 127 for positives (1 to 127).

In binary, 10000000 is -128 and 01111111 is 127. The same asymmetry explains why Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) is still negative.

code.title: Silent overflow vs addExact

followUps:
No. A negative result catches only some overflows, and many wrapped values still look positive. For 13! the true value is 6,227,020,800, and as an int it wraps to 1,932,053,504, which is positive and wrong.

Also, adding two large positives can wrap to a negative, but multiplying can wrap to any sign. Reliable checks are Math.multiplyExact, widening to long, or comparing bounds before the operation.

It does the operation in a wider type and checks whether the result still fits. Conceptually: long r = (long) x + (long) y; if ((int) r != r) throw new ArithmeticException("integer overflow");

For long values it uses a bit trick instead: overflow happened if both operands have the same sign and the result has a different sign, that is ((x ^ r) & (y ^ r)) < 0. The JIT turns this into a single hardware overflow check.

Floating point does not wrap and does not throw. It goes to Infinity or -Infinity: Double.MAX_VALUE * 2 gives Infinity, and 1.0 / 0 is also Infinity. Operations like 0.0 / 0 or Infinity - Infinity give NaN.

Tiny values underflow toward 0.0 gradually. Check with Double.isInfinite(x) and Double.isNaN(x), since NaN == NaN is false.

code.title: Widening, narrowing and compound assignment

followUps:
(int) 3.99 is 3, (int) -3.99 is -3, and (int) Double.NaN is 0. Casting a floating value to int truncates toward zero, it does not round, and NaN becomes 0.

Values too large saturate: (int) 1e20 is Integer.MAX_VALUE and (int) -1e20 is Integer.MIN_VALUE. To round to the nearest, use Math.round(3.99), which returns 4.

Because a method call needs an exact match or a widening conversion, and an integer literal like 10 has type int, which would be a narrowing to byte. Assignment allows narrowing of constants, method invocation does not.

static void f(byte b) {}
f(10);        // error
f((byte) 10); // ok
byte x = 10;  // ok, assignment

The same applies to short and char parameters.

With the literal 0 the conditional expression has type char, so it prints X. With an int variable, as in false ? i : x, it undergoes numeric promotion to int and prints 88.

Rule: if one operand is char and the other is an int constant that fits in char, the result is char. A non-constant int operand forces the result to int. This is why the same-looking code prints different things.

code.title: Why warm-up matters for timing

followUps:
Deoptimization is the JVM throwing away optimized machine code and going back to the interpreter because an assumption made by the JIT stopped being true. For example, the JIT assumed a call site only ever saw one class and inlined it, then a second class appears.

Other triggers are a branch never taken before suddenly being taken, or a class loading that breaks a type assumption. It is safe but causes a temporary slowdown while the code is profiled and recompiled.

Because the first runs happen in the interpreter or in low-tier compiled code, so timing includes the slow start, and the JIT may also remove code whose result is never used. A single timed loop of 1 million calls may measure interpretation, not the steady state.

Use JMH, which runs warm-up iterations, forks fresh JVMs, and uses a blackhole to keep results alive. Report the steady-state numbers, not the first run.

Native-image gives startup in tens of milliseconds and a lower memory footprint, but it needs closed-world analysis. JIT gives better peak throughput on long running services and full dynamic features.

  • Native: fast start, small RSS, no warm-up; but reflection and proxies need configuration, builds take minutes, and no runtime profile optimization.
  • JIT: slower start (seconds), more memory, but adapts to real traffic and has better debugging tools.

Pick native for functions and CLIs, JIT for long running servers.

code.title: i = i++ keeps the old value

followUps:
Predict: x++ gives 5 (x becomes 6), ++x makes x 7 and gives 7, then x-- gives 7 (x becomes 6). So y = 5 + 7 * 7 = 54, and x ends as 6.

Java evaluates operands strictly left to right, and multiplication binds tighter than addition, but each operand is still evaluated in order. This is well defined, unlike in C, but nobody should write it.

It sets arr[0] to 2 and i to 2. Java evaluates the array reference and index expression first, so the index is fixed to 0 before the right side is evaluated; then i = 2 runs, and the value 2 is stored into arr[0].

int[] arr = new int[3]; int i = 0;
arr[i] = i = 2;
// arr = {2, 0, 0}, i = 2

In C the same line is undefined behaviour.

code.title: double vs BigDecimal

followUps:
Because float has only about 7 significant digits, and the rounding error in 0.1f + 0.2f happens to round to the same float as 0.3f, so the printout is the shortest text that identifies it, 0.3. With double the error is visible, giving 0.30000000000000004.

It is luck, not accuracy: 0.1f + 0.2f == 0.3f may be true, but 0.1f * 3 == 0.3f can differ. Never rely on it.

equals compares value and scale, so new BigDecimal("1.0").equals(new BigDecimal("1.00")) is false, while compareTo compares only the numeric value and returns 0.

This matters in HashSet and HashMap: 1.0 and 1.00 become two keys. Use compareTo(...) == 0 for numeric equality, or normalize with stripTrailingZeros() first.

Banks usually use HALF_EVEN, also called banker's rounding: ties round to the nearest even digit, so the rounding errors cancel out over many transactions. Example: 2.5 becomes 2, 3.5 becomes 4, and 2.4 or 2.6 round normally.

With HALF_UP, ties always go up, so a million 0.5 values would drift upward by 500,000. In Java use setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN), but follow the rule your business or law requires.

code.title: UTF-16 surrogates and code points

followUps:
Truncate by code points, not by substring on chars, so you never cut a surrogate pair in half. Use int end = name.offsetByCodePoints(0, Math.min(20, name.codePointCount(0, name.length()))); then name.substring(0, end).

For "user-perceived" characters such as family emoji or letters with combining accents, use BreakIterator.getCharacterInstance() instead, since one visible character can be several code points. Also keep a byte limit in mind if the database column is in bytes.

Because Character.isDigit accepts every Unicode decimal digit, such as Arabic-Indic digits (U+0663) and fullwidth digits, not only 0 to 9. So Character.isDigit('\u0663') is true.

It is a problem when validating input, for example an ID or a port, and then calling parse methods or building SQL. Check ASCII explicitly with c >= '0' && c <= '9'. Note that Integer.parseInt also accepts these digits.

code.title: Startup sequence of a Java program

followUps:
Usually a typo in the class name, the wrong classpath, or a package mismatch. The launcher searches the classpath for the exact fully qualified name.

  • Class name misspelled or given with .class or a slash.
  • Missing directory in -cp, or compiled output not there.
  • Package declaration does not match the folder: com.acme.App must be in com/acme/App.class.
  • Wrong JDK version (class compiled for a newer Java gives a different error, UnsupportedClassVersionError).

Because a non-daemon thread is still running, for example a thread pool created with Executors.newFixedThreadPool that was never shut down. The JVM only exits when all non-daemon threads end.

Fix by calling executor.shutdown(), making worker threads daemon with setDaemon(true), or calling System.exit(0) as a last resort. A thread dump with jcmd <pid> Thread.print shows which thread keeps it alive.

Nothing. Shutdown hooks run on normal exit, System.exit, Ctrl+C (SIGINT) and SIGTERM, but SIGKILL (kill -9) cannot be caught, so the process dies instantly with no hooks, no finally blocks and no flushing.

An out of memory kill or power loss behaves the same. So make important work crash safe with transactions or write-ahead logs, and keep hooks short, since containers give only about 10 to 30 seconds after SIGTERM.

code.title: StackOverflowError vs OutOfMemoryError

followUps:
The heap and Metaspace need garbage collection or class unloading; the thread stacks, PC registers and native stacks do not. Stack frames are freed automatically when a method returns.

  • Heap: collected by the GC, objects die when unreachable.
  • Metaspace: freed only when a class loader becomes unreachable.
  • Stacks: popped on return, no GC.
  • Direct buffers: freed when their owner object is collected or cleaned.

Modern JVMs read the container's cgroup limit and size the heap from it. By default the maximum heap is 25% of the container memory, which is small, so set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 for services where heap is the main user.

Example: a 2 GB container with 75% gives a 1.5 GB heap; the remaining 0.5 GB must cover Metaspace, thread stacks, code cache and direct buffers. If the sum exceeds the limit, the kernel kills the container (OOMKilled).

Yes, in effect. When escape analysis proves an object never leaves a method, the JIT can use scalar replacement: the fields live in registers or on the stack and no heap object is allocated. For example, a new Point(1,2) used only to compute p.x + p.y may cost nothing.

It is an optimization done only by compiled code (C2), not guaranteed, and the language still says the object is on the heap. Do not rely on it for correctness.

code.title: Shifts and the binary search midpoint bug

followUps:
Because the midpoint only works when lo and hi are non-negative. With negative values, the unsigned shift treats the sum's bits as a huge positive number, so the answer is wrong.

Example: lo = -4, hi = -2: sum = -6, -6 >>> 1 = 2147483645, while the real midpoint is -3. Array indexes are never negative, so it is fine for binary search. For general values use lo + (hi - lo) / 2 or Math.floorDiv.

HashMap uses it to spread hash bits: (h = key.hashCode()) ^ (h >>> 16). The table index is only the low bits of the hash, so XOR with the high 16 bits makes those bits depend on the whole hash.

Example: hash codes 0x10000 and 0x20000 both have low 16 bits zero, so in a 16-slot table they collide; after mixing they land in different buckets. The unsigned shift is needed so the sign does not smear in 1s.

code.title: Narrowing a long ID to int

followUps:
Migrate in expand and contract steps so old and new code work at once. Steps: add a nullable BIGINT column, deploy code writing both, backfill in batches (for example 10,000 rows at a time), add the index concurrently, switch reads to the new column, then drop the old one.

ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN id_big BIGINT;
-- backfill in batches, then:
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ... (id_big);

Tools like pt-online-schema-change or gh-ost do the copy with triggers. Foreign keys must be widened too.

Because JavaScript numbers are 64-bit doubles that hold integers exactly only up to 2^53 (9,007,199,254,740,992). A larger ID gets rounded to the nearest representable value, so two different IDs can become the same.

Example: JSON.parse('9007199254740993') yields 9007199254740992. Send 64-bit IDs as strings in JSON, or use BigInt in the client.

Anything that only goes up: auto-increment keys, event sequence numbers, byte counters, cumulative message counts, timestamps in milliseconds stored in an int (2038 problem for seconds), and loop counters in long running processes.

Example: a 32-bit counter at 10,000 events per second overflows after about 2.1 billion / 10,000 = 214,748 seconds, roughly 2.5 days. Use long, and alert when a counter passes 70% of its range.

Native-image is the wrong choice when you depend on heavy reflection, dynamic class loading or agents, when peak throughput on a long running service matters, or when build time and debugging cost outweigh startup gains.

  • Libraries that generate classes at runtime or load plugins dynamically.
  • A service running for days where C2 optimization beats AOT code.
  • Teams who need JFR, jcmd or hot patching features that are limited in native images.

A normal JVM with a Leyden AOT cache is often enough.

Set the container limit first, then give the heap a share and leave room for everything else. A common rule is a heap of 50 to 75% of the limit, set with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage.

Example: 1 GB limit, heap 650 MB (65%), leaving 350 MB for Metaspace (about 100 MB), thread stacks (200 threads x 1 MB = 200 MB, fewer with virtual threads), code cache and direct buffers. Check with Native Memory Tracking (-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary) and load test; if the container is OOMKilled, the heap share is too high.

It reads the compiled bytecode and tells you which JDK modules and classes your code really uses, even when they are not declared in pom.xml. The pom lists library dependencies, not which of the 70 or so JDK modules, like java.sql or jdk.unsupported, you need.

Use jdeps --print-module-deps app.jar to get the list and pass it to jlink --add-modules. It also warns about internal API use and split packages.
